claims.text: The initial high-entropy alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
The initial alloy has a favorable strength–ductility combination.
Introducing a controlled amount of grain-boundary-pinning particles will preserve toughness after thermal exposure and loading.
The intervention is the introduction of grain-boundary-pinning particles.
The applicable thermal exposure is 700°C for 1000 hours.
The post-exposure loading regime is tensile loading at room temperature.
Grain-boundary-pinning particles will inhibit grain growth during thermal exposure.
Grain-boundary-pinning particles will reduce precipitate formation during thermal exposure.
Precipitates formed during thermal exposure can be detrimental to the alloy's mechanical properties.
Suppressing grain growth and detrimental precipitation will preserve toughness.
The particle-containing alloy will have higher toughness than the same alloy without particles under identical conditions.
The relevant applicability boundaries include exposure temperature, exposure duration, loading rate, and loading magnitude.
The optimal amount and type of pinning particles are uncertain.
Particle distribution and morphology may affect the result.
The proposed experiment compares particle-containing and particle-free alloys after the same thermal exposure and loading.
Toughness, grain size, and precipitate formation will be measured.
Equivalent or lower toughness in the particle-containing alloy relative to the control falsifies the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated loading regime is room-temperature tensile loading, whereas the example toughness measurement is Charpy impact energy, which uses impact rather than tensile loading. The experiment does not clarify which loading mode defines the identical test conditions.
